  "body": "This account is unusually careful: it separates the three faults, tags conjectures as conjectures, flags its own weakest move (o1 against the speculative psychology of c5), and holds open questions open. So the objections below mostly strike at the recommendation layer and at the completeness of the conjecture space. Even where they land, they reorder or extend the account rather than refute its core conjectures — and since they are built from the same thin task text, each is as conjectural as what it targets.

First, a bootstrapping defect. Remedies (1)–(3) — written shared agreements, a standing review, a swap rule — are agreements about how to agree. Installing them requires a negotiation of exactly the kind the account diagnoses as costly and dispute-prone. The account's own point (5) concedes the asker's only lever is their own moves, but that covers the one-on-one outreach, not the institutional pieces, which need buy-in from both other flatmates. If this holds, the list needs ordering by unilateral feasibility — personal record-keeping, a proposed zone split the asker simply declares they will follow, async outreach — with the shared institutions treated as proposals contingent on that work, not as the core fix.

Second, an internal tension between c4 and the standing review. The avoider is avoiding the conversations; the review is a recurring three-way conversation. 'Short' is asserted as the fix, but nothing in the text or the account gives grounds that duration, rather than format, outcome, or anticipated blame, is what is being avoided. Unless the one-on-one establishes that, the load-bearing element should be specified as asynchronous or opt-in.

Third, remedy (3) undercuts c3. Fixed zones are still allocations, and by the account's own analysis allocations decay when schedules change. Zones only stay current if the review works — so the five points are not independent remedies, and nearly all the load lands on the element most exposed to the avoidance fault. If the review is rejected, the account has no fallback.

Fourth, the conjecture space for 'we disagree about what the agreement meant' is incomplete. Besides underspecification and quiet re-tailoring when circumstances change, retrospective excuse-manufacture after plain non-performance fits the text equally well — ambiguity produced on demand because producing it costs nothing. And 'we wrote' is not innocent: written words still get interpreted, and control of the shared record becomes a fresh negotiable surface. Written agreements still help under this reading (they raise the cost of on-demand ambiguity), but expectations change: disputes get relocated more than settled, and the account says nothing about what happens when a written agreement is still not met.

Fifth, the option space is tacitly limited to better governance of the shared chore stock. Dissolving interdependence — each person handles their own dishes and mess, a paid clean of common areas split three ways if affordable, or a consciously lower shared standard — is never considered, though the account's own diagnosis (negotiation is expensive, one party opts out) fits shrink-the-surface remedies as well as or better than mechanism design. At minimum the account should say why governance rather than dissolution.

One open question: the task is a first-person participant's account — 'we keep arguing' — so the reporter is inside the disputes and could be part of what the avoider avoids. Neither the text nor the account can settle this, but the account treats the asker as a neutral repair agent throughout. What survives all this: the three-fault separation, the mechanism-over-allocation framing, and the asynchronous, forward-looking outreach to the avoider. My criticisms may be mistaken in the same directions I allege against the account.",

Work on the problem using the material actually exposed in this request and your background knowledge. The problem has no supplied answer key or scoring rule. Claims, criticisms and methods are fallible. Do not invent a source, an observation, an earlier event, or a dependency to fill a field. A missing view says what you can currently see; it does not establish what happened earlier. Return a JSON object with exactly two independently authored string fields: body and commitments. Body is your public prose contribution. Commitments says what taking your contribution up would involve. An empty commitment surface is allowed when none can be identified. Do not repeat the body wholesale into commitments.

Use FCL-1 for the commitment surface, encoded as a JSON document inside the commitments string: {"language":"FCL-1","records":[...],"uptake":[...]}. Each record has unique local id, type (claim|commitment|objection|use|problem), and text (unrestricted prose). Optional prose fields: scope, action, consequence, grounds, bearing. Optional arrays of references: target, depends, mentions, revises, withdraws. References are local IDs or exposed-artifact-label#local-ID; do not invent hidden IDs. A commitment proposes a scoped use, action, application or consequence; an objection alleges a defect whose bearing can itself be criticized; a use proposes an uptake or response; a problem states an unresolved question. depends asserts reliance; mentions only locates material. uptake lists the records you currently propose to use, not certified truths. No record type or optional field must be present. Empty records and uptake are allowed. Express uncertainty or an unrepresentable relation in prose rather than inventing a relation. The body remains unrestricted prose.

Return one JSON object with exactly two string fields: "body" and "commitments". Write the actual commitments separately; do not copy the body into that field as a storage shortcut.

# objection

Develop criticism of the account where you have grounds. It is possible that your objection, its relevance, or the problem formulation is mistaken.

## Original problem (task)
[01274f41553299e7] (h005.task.v1)
I share a flat with two friends. We keep arguing about ordinary household chores. Sometimes we agree on who will do something, but later we disagree about what the agreement meant. Our work schedules change, and one friend has started avoiding the conversations. What should I do?

## Selected input account (p.objection.0)

BODY
An account of the problem, built from the task text alone. The selected previous input (p.account.0) exposed no readable content to this invocation, so this begins fresh rather than continuing anything.

The situation contains three separate faults braided together, and separating them matters because they need different handling.

First, meaning drift: agreements get made, then read differently later. My main conjecture is underspecification — "I'll sort the dishes" leaves open by when, how often, and what counts as done, so each person fills the gaps from their own memory and convenience. Worth holding a second conjecture alongside: the ambiguity may be doing work, letting people quietly re-tailor commitments when schedules change, in which case the fight about meaning is really a displaced fight about the changed circumstances.

Second, a moving target: schedules change, so any one-off division of labour decays. Conjecture: the flat has allocations but no allocation mechanism — no routine, low-friction way to revise who does what — so every schedule change forces a fresh full negotiation, and every negotiation is a new chance to argue. If that is right, renegotiating the current split solves nothing durable; the repair has to be at the level of process.

Third, withdrawal: one friend is avoiding the conversations. Conjecture: avoidance is information about the conversation, not only about the chores. Readings that fit: the talks keep turning into disputes about what was said; the avoider expects to lose or to be held later to ambiguities; or their schedule makes any commitment feel like a trap. Any remedy requiring a long three-way summit is structurally mismatched to this fault.

Two weaker conjectures as amplifiers rather than explanations: people reliably notice their own contributions more than others', so all three flatmates may sincerely feel over-burdened; and chore rows often proxy for fairness and respect, so winning an argument rarely settles the feeling. I flag these as speculative — the practical direction below does not depend on them.

What follows for action, conjecturally: (1) recast "what did we agree" fights as specification bugs and write agreements somewhere shared — what, by when, and what done means — turning "you said" into "we wrote"; (2) install a short standing review (fifteen minutes every week or two) so schedule changes get absorbed routinely, with a default rule for missed slots — swap with a named person rather than quietly skip; (3) shrink the negotiable surface by assigning zones or recurring ownership instead of re-deciding task by task; (4) approach the avoider one-on-one, briefly, possibly in writing, asking what would make these exchanges easier rather than why they have been absent; (5) accept that the asker's lever is their own moves — the format they propose and how they respond when a meaning dispute starts — not control of the other two.

Open questions the task text cannot settle, and which a continuer should keep open: whether the avoider is currently doing more or less than their share; whether a specific incident triggered the withdrawal; and whether the three even share a standard of "clean" and "done" — if standards diverge, perfectly recorded agreements will still breed disputes.
COMMITMENTS
